y-m-12-01.title: The protractor has two rows of marks and it's confusing
y-m-12-01.topic: Measuring the size of an angle with a protractor (reading two rows of marks)
y-m-12-01.goal: Find a standard for deciding which number to read from the two rows of marks on a protractor, and correct a wrong reading by checking it against an estimated size.
y-m-12-01.material: Minjae is measuring the size of angle ㅅㅇㅈ (시옷 이응 지읒), drawn on paper, with a protractor. He lined up the center of the protractor with the vertex ㅇ, and lined up side ㅇㅅ with the 0° mark on the right of the protractor. Looking at where side ㅇㅈ passes, the marks can be read in two rows. Reading the row that starts from the right 0° gives 65, and reading the row that starts from the left 0° gives 115. This angle looks narrower than a right angle (the right-angle corner of a set square). The picture is not shown, so imagine the positions described in words.
y-m-12-01.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in a solution
y-m-12-01.thinking.1: Checking the result by estimating (comparing with a right angle)
y-m-12-01.thinking.2: Checking that when the situation changes, the same method gives a different result
y-m-12-01.prereq.0: Experience measuring angles with a protractor (4th grade)
y-m-12-01.prereq.1: A right angle is 90°, an angle smaller than a right angle is an acute angle, and a bigger one is an obtuse angle
y-m-12-01.s.s1.prompt: Minjae wrote the process of measuring the angle one line at a time. Choose the one line that has a mistake.
y-m-12-01.s.s1.hint.0: First find which 0° the aligned side was placed on in the protractor.
y-m-12-01.s.s1.hint.1: Follow the row of marks that starts from that 0° with your finger and check which of 65 and 115 is a number in that row.
y-m-12-01.s.s1.line.0: Line up the center of the protractor with the vertex ㅇ.
y-m-12-01.s.s1.line.1: Line up side ㅇㅅ with the 0° mark on the right of the protractor.
y-m-12-01.s.s1.line.2: The mark that side ㅇㅈ points to can be read in two rows, giving 65 and 115.
y-m-12-01.s.s1.line.3: 115 is the bigger number and stands out more, so I choose 115.
y-m-12-01.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is wrong. Which number to read is decided not by 'which number is bigger' but by which 0° the aligned side is on. Side ㅇㅅ was aligned with the right 0°, so you must read the row that starts from the right 0°, and this also matches the estimate that the angle is narrower than a right angle. Line 5 is a result that carries over the mistake of line 4.
y-m-12-01.s.s2.prompt: I measured another angle the same way. This time too, one side was aligned with the right 0°, and this angle looks much wider than a right angle. Reading the row that starts from the right 0° gives 105, and reading the row that starts from the left 0° gives 75. Which value is suitable?
y-m-12-01.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether an angle wider than a right angle should be a number bigger than 90 or smaller than 90.
y-m-12-01.s.s2.hint.1: Compare side by side whether the correct value was the bigger number or the smaller number in the previous question and in this question.
y-m-12-01.s.s2.o.a: 75°: The smaller number was right in the previous question, so I choose the smaller number this time too
y-m-12-01.s.s2.r.a: You carried over the result of the previous question as if it were a rule. The rule is not 'the smaller number' but which 0° it started from.
y-m-12-01.s.s2.o.d: Cannot decide: because both numbers are written on the protractor
y-m-12-01.s.s2.r.d: Even if both numbers are written, you can decide on one if you use a standard (the aligned 0°, the estimate).
y-m-12-01.s.s2.explain: This time, 105 in the row that starts from the right 0° is suitable. In the previous question the smaller number was right, and this time the bigger number is right. So the standard must be not the size of the number but 'the row that starts from the aligned 0°' and 'whether it is wider or narrower than a right angle'.
y-m-12-01.s.s3.prompt: A friend says the marks are in two rows and they don't know which number to read. Write a method for how to decide and tell them. If you think of two methods, you may write both.
y-m-12-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write what 'checking question' could cross out one of the two numbers.
y-m-12-01.s.s3.hint.1: Solve the previous two questions again with this method and polish your sentences.
y-m-12-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Read the row that starts from the aligned 0°, and check by comparing with a right angle.
y-m-12-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did your method state a standard, rather than deciding by the size of the number like 'the bigger number is right / the smaller number is right'?
y-m-12-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Can your method explain both of the previous questions (65 and 105)?
y-m-12-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: If you used two methods, did you check that they point to the same number?
y-m-12-01.s.s3.model.0: Read the number in the row that starts from the 0° mark where you aligned the side. If you aligned it with the right 0°, read the row that starts from the right 0°. And look to see whether the angle is wider or narrower than a right angle, and check once more that it is right.
y-m-12-01.s.s3.model.1: First estimate whether the angle is narrower or wider than a right angle. If it is narrower, you must choose the number less than 90, and if it is wider, the number greater than 90, so only one of the two numbers is left.
y-m-12-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is a method that lets you choose one using only an estimate, without mentioning the 0° side.

y-m-12-02.title: Shapes you can make with a 30 cm wire
y-m-12-02.topic: The number of sides of a regular polygon and the length of one side (when the wire length is fixed)
y-m-12-02.goal: Using the relationship between the number of sides and the length of one side of a regular polygon when the total wire length is fixed, make several cases that fit the conditions and explain what changes when the conditions change.
y-m-12-02.material: There is a wire that is 30 cm long. You want to use all of this wire, with none left over and no overlapping, to make one regular polygon. The conditions are set like this. The number of sides is 3 or more, and the length of one side is a natural number of cm. A side of 1 cm is too short and hard to bend, so make each side 2 cm or more. Do not think about the thickness of the wire or the parts that are joined. Mina said, “With 30 cm you can make an equilateral triangle and also a square.”
y-m-12-02.thinking.0: Reading the conditions (natural number, 2 cm or more) and finding all possible cases
y-m-12-02.thinking.2: Judging whether the conclusion changes when the conditions change
y-m-12-02.prereq.0: Regular polygons (polygons with all side lengths and all angle sizes equal)
y-m-12-02.prereq.1: Calculating with multiplication and division (cases that divide evenly)
y-m-12-02.s.s1.prompt: Are Mina's words right under the conditions above?
y-m-12-02.s.s1.hint.0: An equilateral triangle has 3 sides, all the same length. Divide the 30 cm wire equally into 3 and find how long one side is.
y-m-12-02.s.s1.hint.1: For a square too, find one side in the same way, and then check whether that number fits the condition 'natural number of cm'.
y-m-12-02.s.s1.o.a: Right. As long as you use all the wire, you can make any regular polygon
y-m-12-02.s.s1.r.a: You only checked that all the wire is used. Also check the condition that the length of one side must be a natural number.
y-m-12-02.s.s1.o.b: An equilateral triangle is not possible and a square is possible. The one with more sides is easier to make
y-m-12-02.s.s1.r.b: Having more sides does not make it work. Calculate for yourself how long one side becomes in each.
y-m-12-02.s.s1.o.c: An equilateral triangle is possible and a square is not possible because one side is 7.5 cm
y-m-12-02.s.s1.r.c: You found the length of one side of the equilateral triangle and the square and checked against the conditions.
y-m-12-02.s.s1.o.d: No matter how many sides, the wire length is 30, so one side is always 10 cm
y-m-12-02.s.s1.r.d: When the number of sides changes, the length of one side changes too. It is 10 cm only for an equilateral triangle.
y-m-12-02.s.s1.explain: For an equilateral triangle, one side is 30 divided by 3, which is 10 cm, so it fits the conditions. For a square, one side is 7.5 cm, but 7.5 is not a natural number, so it is not possible under these conditions. If you change the condition to 'decimal cm are also allowed', a square is possible too.
y-m-12-02.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different regular polygons that can be made under these conditions. Write the number of sides n and the length of one side s (cm).
y-m-12-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a number of sides, and divide the wire equally by that number to find how long one side is.
y-m-12-02.s.s2.hint.1: If it does not divide evenly, one side is not a natural number. Try in the order 3, 4, 5, 6, ....
y-m-12-02.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of sides is a natural number that is 3 or more.
y-m-12-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of sides must be a natural number that is 3 or more.
y-m-12-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The length of one side is a natural number that is 2 cm or more.
y-m-12-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The length of one side must be a natural number that is 2 cm or more.
y-m-12-02.s.s2.ok.c3: Use all 30 cm of the wire.
y-m-12-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The perimeter calculated from the number of sides and the length of one side is not 30 cm.
y-m-12-02.s.s2.explain: The possible cases are 3 sides (10 cm), 5 sides (6 cm), 6 sides (5 cm), 10 sides (3 cm), and 15 sides (2 cm), 5 in all. With 30 sides, one side would be 1 cm, which does not fit the conditions, and with 2 sides or fewer, it does not make a shape.
y-m-12-02.s.s3.prompt: The wire changed to 29 cm. Can you make a regular polygon under the same conditions (3 or more sides, one side a natural number of cm that is 2 cm or more)? Write your conclusion and reason, and also write whether it changes if you change the conditions.
y-m-12-02.s.s3.hint.0: Compare what relationship the numbers of sides that were possible with 30 cm had with 30.
y-m-12-02.s.s3.hint.1: Check from 3, one at a time, whether there is a number (other than 1 and 29) that divides 29 evenly.
y-m-12-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you go through the process of dividing 29 by the number of sides and the length of one side?
y-m-12-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: In 'if you change the conditions' (example: decimal cm allowed), did you write specifically what cases become possible?
y-m-12-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain why it is different compared with the 30 cm case?
y-m-12-02.s.s3.model.0: It can't be made. 29 divides evenly only by 1 and 29, and with 29 sides, one side would be 1 cm, which does not fit the conditions. If decimal cm are fine for one side, a square can be made with one side of 7.25 cm.
y-m-12-02.s.s3.model.1: It can't. If you divide 29 by 3, 4, 5, 6 as in the 30 cm case, none of them divides evenly. If you remove the natural-number condition, you can make it with 3 sides by making one side the length of 29 divided by 3.
y-m-12-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that was checked by dividing.

y-m-12-03.title: How many degrees is angle ㄱㅇㄷ?
y-m-12-03.topic: Sum and difference of the sizes of angles (when the rays are in different positions)
y-m-12-03.goal: Judge whether one value is fixed by the given information alone, say what more information is needed for the value to be fixed as just one, and make angles that fit the conditions in both cases.
y-m-12-03.material: From point ㅇ, three rays ㅇㄱ, ㅇㄴ, ㅇㄷ were drawn. Angle ㄱㅇㄴ is 40° and angle ㄴㅇㄷ is 30°. All three rays are within the same side of a straight line (a range smaller than 180°). The picture is not shown, and you are not told in what order the rays are placed. Minsu said, “Angle ㄱㅇㄷ is 70°, putting 40° and 30° together.”
y-m-12-03.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-12-03.thinking.2: Checking whether additional information reduces the cases
y-m-12-03.prereq.0: Expressing the size of an angle in degrees (°) (4th grade)
y-m-12-03.prereq.1: Two rays drawn from one point form an angle
y-m-12-03.s.s1.prompt: How would you evaluate Minsu's words from the given information alone?
y-m-12-03.s.s1.hint.0: Draw ray ㅇㄴ first, then draw ㅇㄱ opening 40° from it and ㅇㄷ opening 30° from it. You can draw ㅇㄷ on the opposite side of ㅇㄱ, or on the same side.
y-m-12-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how many degrees angle ㄱㅇㄷ is in each of the two drawings.
y-m-12-03.s.s1.o.a: It is 70°. The two angles are connected, so you just put them together
y-m-12-03.s.s1.r.a: You assumed the two angles are connected in the picture. The problem does not give the order of the rays.
y-m-12-03.s.s1.o.b: It could be 70° or 10°, so we need to know more
y-m-12-03.s.s1.r.b: You pointed out that the value can differ depending on the order in which the rays are placed.
y-m-12-03.s.s1.o.c: It is 10°. When comparing angles, you always subtract the smaller angle from the bigger angle
y-m-12-03.s.s1.r.c: Sometimes you subtract, but not always. It depends on where ray ㅇㄴ is.
y-m-12-03.s.s1.o.d: Can't know. You can't say any value before measuring with a protractor
y-m-12-03.s.s1.r.d: Finding all the possible values can be done without measuring.
y-m-12-03.s.s1.explain: If ㅇㄴ is between ㅇㄱ and ㅇㄷ, it is 40°+30°=70°, and if ㅇㄱ and ㅇㄷ are on the same side of ㅇㄴ, it is 10°, the difference between 40° and 30°. The information is lacking, so you can decide only if you know which of the two it is.
y-m-12-03.s.s2.prompt: How many of the following pieces of information, if told to you, would let you fix the size of angle ㄱㅇㄷ as just one value? Choose all that apply.
y-m-12-03.s.s2.hint.0: Check one by one whether 70° and 10° each fit the description in this information.
y-m-12-03.s.s2.hint.1: If both 70° and 10° remain after hearing the information, it is not fixed.
y-m-12-03.s.s2.o.a: Ray ㅇㄴ is between ray ㅇㄱ and ray ㅇㄷ
y-m-12-03.s.s2.r.a: If ㅇㄴ is in the middle, it is fixed as 70°.
y-m-12-03.s.s2.o.b: Angle ㄱㅇㄷ is smaller than a right angle
y-m-12-03.s.s2.r.b: Both 70° and 10° are smaller than a right angle, so it cannot separate the two cases.
y-m-12-03.s.s2.o.c: Rays ㅇㄱ and ㅇㄷ are on the same side of ray ㅇㄴ
y-m-12-03.s.s2.r.c: If they are on the same side, it is fixed as 10°.
y-m-12-03.s.s2.o.d: Angle ㄱㅇㄴ is bigger than angle ㄴㅇㄷ
y-m-12-03.s.s2.r.d: It is already given information (40° > 30°), so it tells nothing new.
y-m-12-03.s.s2.r.e: 10° is smaller than 30°, so with this information only one case remains.
y-m-12-03.s.s2.explain: a fixes it as 70° and c fixes it as 10°. e also leaves only 70°, because 10° is not bigger than 30°, so it is fixed. b is true in both cases, and d is already known, so it does not reduce the cases.
y-m-12-03.s.s3.prompt: Make 3 different cases in which angle ㄱㅇㄷ is a right angle (90°). Write angle ㄱㅇㄴ as p and angle ㄴㅇㄷ as q (in degrees). You may write both cases made by a sum and cases made by a difference. All angles are natural numbers, greater than 0° and less than 180°.
y-m-12-03.s.s3.hint.0: Think about what the two angles must add up to for them to make 90° when placed together.
y-m-12-03.s.s3.hint.1: For the case where they are placed overlapping on one side, find pairs where the bigger angle minus the smaller angle is 90°.
y-m-12-03.s.s3.ok.c1: Both angles are greater than 0° and less than 180°.
y-m-12-03.s.s3.fail.c1: An angle must be greater than 0° and less than 180°.
y-m-12-03.s.s3.fail.c2: Write the size of an angle as a natural number of degrees.
y-m-12-03.s.s3.ok.c3: The sum or the difference of the two angles is 90°.
y-m-12-03.s.s3.fail.c3: Neither the sum nor the difference is 90°.
y-m-12-03.s.s3.explain: There are cases where the sum is 90° (example: 50° and 40°) and cases where the difference is 90° (example: 100° and 10°). Pairs with p and q swapped count as the same example.

y-m-12-04.title: The grounds for saying 'all quadrilaterals'
y-m-12-04.topic: Comparing the grounds that explain the sum of the four angles of a quadrilateral
y-m-12-04.goal: Compare, as grounds for talking about 'all shapes', data obtained by measuring and an explanation obtained by splitting the shape, decide which is more suitable, and apply the same method to a new shape.
y-m-12-04.material: Sua and Junho are talking about whether 'the sum of the four angles of a quadrilateral is 360°' is right for all quadrilaterals. Think only about quadrilaterals with no dent going inward. Sua: 'I measured 5 quadrilaterals with a protractor and added the four angles, and got 359°, 361°, 360°, 362°, 358°. So the sum of every quadrilateral is 360°.' Junho: 'If you draw one diagonal in a quadrilateral, it splits into two triangles. The sum of the three angles of one triangle is 180°, so the sum of the four angles of a quadrilateral is 360°.'
y-m-12-04.thinking.0: Comparing kinds of grounds (measured data and an explanation with reasons)
y-m-12-04.thinking.1: Judging the meaning of measurement error
y-m-12-04.thinking.2: Extending a method you know to a new shape
y-m-12-04.prereq.0: The sum of the three angles of a triangle is 180°
y-m-12-04.prereq.1: The meaning of quadrilateral and diagonal (a line segment joining two vertices that are not next to each other)
y-m-12-04.prereq.2: We only deal with quadrilaterals that have no dent going inward
y-m-12-04.s.s1.prompt: Compare the two friends' explanations as grounds for speaking about 'all quadrilaterals'. Which is more suitable?
y-m-12-04.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether you can guarantee that measuring a 6th quadrilateral with Sua's method will give exactly 360°.
y-m-12-04.s.s1.hint.1: Draw one more quadrilateral and try Junho's explanation on it to see whether it can be used as it is for any quadrilateral.
y-m-12-04.s.s1.o.a: Sua's explanation is better. She measured as many as five quadrilaterals herself and all the results were near 360°
y-m-12-04.s.s1.r.a: Measuring is a valuable check, but it is hard to say all quadrilaterals are the same just because five were measured. There remains a chance that the next quadrilateral is different.
y-m-12-04.s.s1.o.b: The two explanations are the same level of grounds. Both say the same result, that the sum is 360°
y-m-12-04.s.s1.r.b: Even if the results are the same, whether they show 'why it is so' is different. Compare which explanation can be used as it is for a new quadrilateral.
y-m-12-04.s.s1.o.c: Neither is a ground. You cannot measure all quadrilaterals, and the explanation is also just a few examples
y-m-12-04.s.s1.r.c: Even if you cannot measure all of them, explaining with a reason lets you speak about all cases at once. Look at whether Junho's explanation is like that.
y-m-12-04.s.s1.o.d: Junho's explanation is a ground. Any quadrilateral can be split by a diagonal, and Sua's measuring is for checking
y-m-12-04.s.s1.r.d: You pointed out why the method applies to all quadrilaterals in the same way, and kept measuring as a check.
y-m-12-04.s.s1.explain: Junho's explanation relies on the fact that any (non-dented) quadrilateral can be split into two triangles by a diagonal, so it supports 'all'. Sua's measuring can be used to check that the explanation is right. But note that Junho's explanation also trusts that 'the sum of the three angles of a triangle is 180°'.
y-m-12-04.s.s2.prompt: When Sua measured, there were also quadrilaterals whose sums were 358° and 362°. How is it good to understand this result?
y-m-12-04.s.s2.hint.0: Count how many of the five values are on the smaller side and on the bigger side of 360.
y-m-12-04.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether measuring the same quadrilateral twice gives exactly the same value.
y-m-12-04.s.s2.o.a: Values measured with a protractor can differ by about 1~2°, so the results came out near 360°
y-m-12-04.s.s2.r.a: You understood it as common measurement error. It is also evidence that the size of the error is small and spreads on both sides of 360°.
y-m-12-04.s.s2.o.b: It is proof that there are quadrilaterals whose sum is not 360°. Because the values 358° and 362° really came out
y-m-12-04.s.s2.r.b: 358° and 362° stray by a similar amount on both sides. Compare whether they keep straying only to one side.
y-m-12-04.s.s2.o.c: It is proof that Junho's explanation is wrong. Because the measured values are not exactly equal to the value found by the explanation
y-m-12-04.s.s2.r.c: Junho's explanation is an explanation with reasons, so it is hard to say right away that it is wrong just because a few measured values are slightly different.
y-m-12-04.s.s2.o.d: Measuring with a protractor must always give exactly 360°, so every value that is not 360° was measured wrongly
y-m-12-04.s.s2.r.d: Differences from reading the marks are common. It is more likely an error than a wrong measurement.
y-m-12-04.s.s2.explain: Measured values commonly differ by 1~2° because of the way of reading and the marks. 358°, 359°, 361°, 362° are scattered on both sides of 360°, so it is natural to see them as errors. But you cannot conclude 'exactly 360°' from measuring alone, so an explanation with reasons is also needed.
y-m-12-04.s.s3.prompt: Continue Junho's method. What is the sum of the five angles of a pentagon with no dent going inward? Write how you found it. It is fine if your method is different.
y-m-12-04.s.s3.hint.0: Choose one vertex of the pentagon, draw diagonals from that vertex to the other vertices, and count how many triangles are formed.
y-m-12-04.s.s3.hint.1: After counting the number of triangles, use the sum of the three angles of one triangle to find the whole.
y-m-12-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is it clear in your method how many triangles you split it into?
y-m-12-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does comparing with another friend's method (the model answer) give the same result?
y-m-12-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can this method be used as it is for other pentagons that have no dent going inward?
y-m-12-04.s.s3.model.0: If you draw two diagonals from one vertex, it splits into 3 triangles. The sum of the angles of one triangle is 180°, so it is 3 times 180°, which is 540°.
y-m-12-04.s.s3.model.1: If you put a point inside the pentagon and join it to the 5 vertices, 5 triangles are formed. 5 times 180° is 900°, but the full turn of 360° around the middle point is not an angle of the pentagon, so subtracting it gives 540°.
y-m-12-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is another method that uses an inside point.
y-m-12-04.s.s3.model.2: If you split the pentagon by a diagonal into one quadrilateral and one triangle, it is 360°+180°=540°.
y-m-12-04.s.s3.modelNote.2: This is a method that uses the already known result for quadrilaterals.

y-m-12-05.title: Are two lines that don't meet parallel?
y-m-12-05.topic: Two parallel lines (the distance between parallel lines)
y-m-12-05.goal: Understand that not meeting inside the paper is not enough to confirm parallel, and revise your judgment while taking into account the error in the distance measurements.
y-m-12-05.material: Line 가 and line 나 are drawn on paper. You want to find out whether the two lines are parallel. The distance between two parallel lines is the length measured perpendicular to line 가, and it is the same wherever you measure. Assume that measuring with a ruler has an error of about 0.2 cm. Measure the distance at places 5 cm apart along line 가. The picture is not shown.
y-m-12-05.thinking.0: Revising your judgment each time data increases
y-m-12-05.thinking.1: Telling apart measurement error and a real difference
y-m-12-05.thinking.2: Choosing ways to make the evidence firmer
y-m-12-05.prereq.0: Parallel: two lines that never meet however far they are extended
y-m-12-05.prereq.1: The distance between two parallel lines is the same wherever you measure
y-m-12-05.prereq.2: Measuring a length with a ruler (a small error occurs)
y-m-12-05.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what you think.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.hint.0: In each step, separate what the new data tells you 'for sure' and what lets you only 'guess'.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.hint.1: To say whether the distances are about the same, compare the difference with the error 0.2 cm.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.0.info: Inside the paper, the two lines do not meet. You cannot extend the lines further beyond the edge of the paper.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: Can we say the two lines are parallel?
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.0.after: Not meeting inside the paper is not enough. If you extend the lines longer, they might meet. You need a way to check (measuring distances, checking perpendicular).
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Parallel. They don't meet, so they are parallel
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: 'They don't meet inside the paper' and 'they never meet however far they are extended' are different.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We can't decide yet. They might meet outside the paper, so we need to check with another method
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You separated what it looks like from what has been confirmed as fact.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Not parallel. If you extend lines long enough they always meet
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Parallel lines never meet however far they are extended.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Can't know. There is no way to check
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: There are ways to check by measuring distances or checking perpendicular.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.1.info: I measured the distance between the two lines at three places 5 cm apart along line 가, and got 4.0 cm, 4.1 cm, 4.0 cm.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.1.after: If the distances at three places are the same within the error range, the chance that they are parallel goes up. But there are only three places, so 'measure more and then decide' is also suitable. Both judgments have grounds.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: They are the same within the error range, so I think they are likely parallel
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You used the fact that the 0.1 cm difference is smaller than the error (about 0.2 cm).
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 4.1 came out, so I conclude they are not parallel
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: A 0.1 cm difference is within the error range. With a difference this size, it is hard to conclude they are not parallel.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: I only measured three places, so I won't decide whether they are parallel until I measure more
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You pointed out that the data is small. Planning to collect more before deciding is also a suitable judgment.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The distances are similar, so the two lines are the same line
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.1.r.d: If the distance is about 4 cm, they are two different lines.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.2.info: A friend drew two other lines, 다 and 라, and I measured them the same way, and the distances were 4.0 cm, 4.6 cm, 5.2 cm. They spread apart by 0.6 cm every 5 cm.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: What do you think about 다 and 라?
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.2.after: The difference is bigger than the error and keeps growing in one direction, so it is suitable to think they are not parallel. If you are worried about the chance of error, measuring again to check is also good. If you go toward the side where the distance shrinks, they will meet someday.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: A difference much bigger than the error (about 0.2 cm) keeps appearing in the same direction, so I think they are not parallel
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You used both that the difference is large and that its direction is constant.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Measured values have error, so I leave it as possibly parallel
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: 0.6 cm is three times the error of 0.2 cm. Moreover, the difference keeps growing in one direction.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: After measuring the same places again to check, if it is the same, I think they are not parallel
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is suitable because it is a plan to check whether the measurement was wrong. If you measure again and get the same value, your judgment will be the same.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.2.o.d: If you keep going toward the side where they spread apart, the two lines meet
y-m-12-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: On the spreading side, the distance gets bigger and bigger and they do not get closer. Think about the side where the distance shrinks.
y-m-12-05.s.s1.reflect: At first you started with 'can't decide', with the second data the 'chance of parallel' went up, and with the third data your judgment changed the other way to 'not parallel'. Notice that although the data was obtained by the same method, your judgment changed depending on whether the difference was bigger or smaller than the error.
y-m-12-05.s.s2.prompt: How many of the following methods make the evidence that 가 and 나 are parallel firmer? Choose all that are suitable.
y-m-12-05.s.s2.hint.0: Recall what property must be true for parallel lines.
y-m-12-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether each method filters out cases that 'happen to look parallel'.
y-m-12-05.s.s2.o.a: Look at them with your eyes for a long time and feel whether they look parallel
y-m-12-05.s.s2.r.a: A feeling from looking is weak evidence. Your eyes can be fooled.
y-m-12-05.s.s2.o.b: Measure the distance at more places
y-m-12-05.s.s2.r.b: The more places you measure, the more you can filter out error or chance at one or two places.
y-m-12-05.s.s2.o.c: Draw one line that passes through both 가 and 나 and check with a set square that both angles are right angles
y-m-12-05.s.s2.r.c: You used the fact that two lines perpendicular to one line are parallel.
y-m-12-05.s.s2.o.d: Check whether the two lines are the same thickness
y-m-12-05.s.s2.r.d: Thickness has nothing to do with being parallel.
y-m-12-05.s.s2.explain: Increasing the places you measure and checking that both are perpendicular to one line make the evidence for parallel firmer. Feeling with your eyes or thickness is only weakly related to parallel.
y-m-12-05.s.s2.acc.0: Increasing the places you measure alone makes the evidence firmer. Checking perpendicular as well is even better.
y-m-12-05.s.s2.acc.1: Checking perpendicular alone is evidence for parallel. Adding measuring is even better.

y-m-12-06.title: Is a flipped shape the same as a turned shape?
y-m-12-06.topic: Comparing the results of flipping and turning a plane shape
y-m-12-06.goal: Find, by testing several shapes, the condition under which flipping up-down and turning 180° give the same result, and make your own shape and predict the result.
y-m-12-06.material: The shapes are made of square cells. A cell that is colored is written ■, and an empty cell is written □. Flipping up-down is the shape reflected in a mirror so that the top and bottom swap (left and right stay the same). Turning 180° is the shape turned half a turn (top goes to bottom, and left goes to right). Yuna said, 'A shape flipped up-down is always the same as the shape turned 180°.'
y-m-12-06.thinking.0: Testing whether a generalization always holds
y-m-12-06.thinking.1: Fixing a claim with a counterexample
y-m-12-06.thinking.2: Guessing the condition and predicting a new case
y-m-12-06.prereq.0: Ways to slide, flip, and turn plane shapes (flip up-down, turn clockwise)
y-m-12-06.prereq.1: Reading shapes made of square cells in words
y-m-12-06.s.s1.prompt: Let's test the shapes one at a time. Each time, choose what you think about Yuna's words.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.hint.0: Follow where one colored cell goes in each of the two moves.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the shapes that were the same (A, C) based on left and right.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.0.info: Shape A is a rectangle of 2 rows and 3 cells with all 6 cells ■. The shape flipped up-down and the shape turned 180° are both rectangles with all 6 cells ■. They are the same.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think now about Yuna's words 'always the same'?
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.0.after: They were the same for A, but if all the cells are colored, it can look the same however you move it, so it is weak evidence. It is suitable to test with other shapes.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It was the same for one shape, so it's fine to believe it is always the same
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: One shape is not enough. All the cells of this shape are colored, so it may be a special case.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It came out the same, but it is a special shape with all cells colored, so I want to test other shapes too
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You tried to examine whether one result is general.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The claim 'always the same' is wrong. Flipping and turning have different names, so the results are different too
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You cannot say the results are different just because the names are different. You have to check with an actual shape.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.0.o.d: I only need to think about rectangles
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.0.r.d: We don't know yet what happens with other shapes.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.1.info: Shape B has 2 rows and 2 cells, in which the upper left, lower left, and lower right cells are ■ and the upper right cell is □ (ㄴ-shape). When flipped up-down, the upper left, upper right, and lower left are ■ and the lower right is □. When turned 180°, the upper left, upper right, and lower right are ■ and the lower left is □.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.1.ask: What happens to Yuna's words now?
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.1.after: B is a counterexample. 'Always the same' is not right if even one case is different. But it is not 'always different' either (they were the same for A).
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: They were different for the ㄴ-shape, so the claim 'always the same' is not right
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You understood that one counterexample breaks 'always'.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The one that came out different was drawn wrongly. They must always be the same
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Checking the drawn result again is good, but if you compare the cell positions directly you can see they really are different.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Only the ㄴ-shape is an exception and the other shapes are always the same
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: One exception has appeared, but there is no ground that all other shapes are the same.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.1.o.d: They were different for the ㄴ-shape, so they are different for every shape
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.1.r.d: They were the same for A. You cannot say they are all different because they were different once.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.2.info: Shape C has 2 rows and 3 cells, in which all 3 cells in the top row are ■ and in the bottom row only the middle cell is ■ (both ends are □) (T shape). When flipped up-down, the 3 cells in the bottom row are ■ and in the top row only the middle is ■. When turned 180° it is the same too. They are the same. Shape D is a shape with 2 rows and 2 cells in which only the upper left cell is ■.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: They were the same for A and C and different for B. Guess whether the two results for D will be the same or different.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.2.after: The difference between flipping up-down and turning 180° is whether left and right swap. For shapes whose left and right are the same like a mirror (A, C), they are the same even when swapped, and for shapes that are not (B, D), they are different. For D, the upper left cell goes to the lower left when flipped and to the lower right when turned.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The same. If there is only one cell, the shape is the same however you move it
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The position of the cell matters. Think about where the upper left cell goes when flipped and where it goes when turned.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Different. Its left and right are not the same like a mirror, so it seems it would be different like B
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You predicted using the difference that A and C are shapes with the same left and right, and B is not.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The same. It has been the same twice and different once so far, so it is likely the same
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Rather than counting the number of times, you should find what the shapes that were the same have in common.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Can't guess. Because it is different for each shape
y-m-12-06.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You can guess from what A and C have in common and how B differs.
y-m-12-06.s.s1.reflect: At first you felt you could judge from just one, but when a counterexample appeared, 'always' was broken. After that, you were able to predict a new shape by finding what the same cases and the different cases have in common. Notice that even after 'always the same' is broken, you can still find 'when they are the same'.
y-m-12-06.s.s2.prompt: Make a shape by choosing ■ cells within 2 rows and 3 cells (say the positions of the cells in words). Predict whether the shape flipped up-down and the shape turned 180° will be the same or different, and also write the reason.
y-m-12-06.s.s2.hint.0: First choose one ■ cell and follow which cell it goes to when flipped up-down and which cell it goes to when turned.
y-m-12-06.s.s2.hint.1: Before predicting, compare the left half and the right half of the shape.
y-m-12-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Can a friend draw exactly the same shape by reading the cell positions of your shape?
y-m-12-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is the reason for your prediction connected to 'whether the left and right are the same shape'?
y-m-12-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: After actually flipping and turning your shape, was your prediction right?
y-m-12-06.s.s2.model.0: Make only the left end cell of the top row and the middle cell of the bottom row ■. Left and right are not the same like a mirror, so the one flipped up-down and the one turned seem to be different.
y-m-12-06.s.s2.model.1: If only the two end cells of the top row are ■, left and right are the same shape like a mirror. So the flipped shape and the turned shape will be the same. In both, the two end cells of the bottom row become ■.
y-m-12-06.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that made the same case.

y-m-12-07.title: Guessing a bean plant's height next week
y-m-12-07.topic: Guessing a value that has not been measured yet from a line graph
y-m-12-07.goal: Estimate the next value from the shape of change in a line graph, but revise your guess and how sure you are when new data arrives.
y-m-12-07.material: Sujin measures the height of a kidney bean sprout once a week at the same time and draws it as a line graph. The unit is cm, and the sprout is grown in the same pot under the same conditions. She wants to guess the height in a week she has not measured yet by looking at the graph. A guess is only 'it could be', not a certainty.
y-m-12-07.thinking.0: Estimating by the pattern of change in the data
y-m-12-07.thinking.1: Revising a guess with new data
y-m-12-07.thinking.2: Evaluating the grounds of a statement that claims something about the distant future
y-m-12-07.prereq.0: How to read a line graph
y-m-12-07.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose how to guess the height for next week.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.hint.0: First compare whether the new data matches the guess so far.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.hint.1: Describe in words the shape of the line joining the points: is it rising, slowing down, or flattening?
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.0.info: Week 1 is 2 cm, week 2 is 4 cm, and week 3 is 6 cm. The points lie on a line that rises straight.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: How do you guess the height in week 4, which has not been measured yet?
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.0.after: If you think the flow of growing 2 cm every week continues, it is about 8 cm. But it is only three measurements, so it is suitable to say 'about'.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is definitely 8 cm. The rule is fixed
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Three measurements do not fix the rule. Tell apart a guess and a certainty.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is 6 cm. It will be the same as the last measured value
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You can see in the data the flow of growing each week. You did not use that flow.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It will probably be about 8 cm. It grew 2 cm every week, so it seems it will continue similarly
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You found the rule of change and estimated, and by saying 'about' you did not fix it as certain.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Can't know. You can't make any guess about the future
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The flow of the data is grounds for a guess. But it is not a certainty.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.1.info: When I measured in week 4, it was 7 cm. Between week 3 and week 4 it grew only 1 cm.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: How do you guess the height in week 5?
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.1.after: From the week 4 data you can see that the first rule does not simply continue. Guesses that use the recent flow (1 cm at a time) or the slowing flow (it might not grow more) are both suitable.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 10 cm. The first rule (2 cm every week) was right, so it continues
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The week 4 data was different from the first rule. Look at whether you reflected the new data in your guess.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Around 8 cm. It grew 1 cm at a time recently, so it seems it will grow about that much
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You revised your guess by reflecting the most recent change.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The week 4 value is strange, so I ignore it and keep 8 cm
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: If you throw away data you don't like, your guess moves away from the data. If you are suspicious, you can measure again.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Around 7 cm. The speed of growing taller is slowing down, so it might not grow more
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You guessed more conservatively from the slowing flow. This also fits the data.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.2.info: In week 5 it was 7 cm, and in week 6 it was 7 cm. They say that because the pot is small, it may not be able to grow beyond some height.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: How do you guess the height in week 7?
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.2.after: There has been almost no change in the last 3 weeks (since week 4), so around 7 cm is suitable. You started from the first rule and revised your guess each time data piled up.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 9 cm. Following the first rule, it will grow 2 cm every week again
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: There was no change for the last three weeks. To use the first rule again, you need a new reason.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 6 cm. It will start to shrink
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: There is no ground in the data that the sprout's height shrinks.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Around 7 cm. Because the height stayed almost the same for the last three weeks
y-m-12-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You reflected the flow of the recent data, and avoided a firm claim with the word 'around'.
y-m-12-07.s.s1.reflect: At first there was a rule, '2 cm every week', but it went off in week 4, and in weeks 5 and 6 it hardly grew. Notice that, in the process of revising the guess each time data increased, you did not stick to the first rule to the end.
y-m-12-07.s.s2.prompt: A friend, Hoyeon, looked only at the data up to week 3 and said, 'In week 10 it will be 20 cm.' How do you see this statement?
y-m-12-07.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether Hoyeon's statement would still be right after receiving the week 4 data and the week 5 data.
y-m-12-07.s.s2.hint.1: Say in one sentence how a guess and a firm claim are different.
y-m-12-07.s.s2.o.a: The grounds are weak. If you claim the distant future from three pieces of data, you can be wrong
y-m-12-07.s.s2.r.a: You told apart a guess and a firm claim, and pointed out that it becomes more uncertain the less data there is and the farther away the time is.
y-m-12-07.s.s2.o.b: Right. It grew 2 cm every week, so after 10 weeks it will be 20 cm
y-m-12-07.s.s2.r.b: You fixed week 10 from the week 3 data. Recall that it went off in week 4.
y-m-12-07.s.s2.o.c: Wrong. A kidney bean sprout is a plant that can't grow beyond 20 cm
y-m-12-07.s.s2.r.c: There is no ground in the data that the plant can't exceed 20 cm. You brought in a fact with no basis.
y-m-12-07.s.s2.o.d: The grounds are weak. Because a line graph can't let you guess anything about the future at all
y-m-12-07.s.s2.r.d: You can guess with a graph. But the farther into the future, the more you can be wrong.
y-m-12-07.s.s2.explain: From the week 3 data, guessing the near week 4 as 'about' is possible, but claiming week 10 firmly has weak grounds. In fact, from week 4 the speed of growth changed. As data piles up, you must revise your guess.

y-m-12-08.title: Same data: which graph is suitable?
y-m-12-08.topic: Choosing between a bar graph and a line graph (matching what you want to do with the data)
y-m-12-08.goal: Understand that the suitable graph can differ depending on what you want to do (compare sizes, see change), and write separately what you can know and cannot know from a graph.
y-m-12-08.material: A class organized in a table the number of books borrowed from the class library each month over the past year. January 42 books, February 18, March 55, April 61, May 58, June 49, July 20, August 12, September 52, October 60, November 63, December 47. You want to show this data in a graph, but each group wants to do something different. Group 가 wants to find the month with the most books borrowed and the month with the fewest. Group 나 wants to see at a glance how the number of books borrowed goes up and down as months pass.
y-m-12-08.thinking.0: Choosing the expression that fits what you want to do
y-m-12-08.thinking.1: Comparing reasons when several answers are possible
y-m-12-08.thinking.2: Telling apart what the data can tell you and what you need to find out more about
y-m-12-08.prereq.0: How to read bar graphs and line graphs
y-m-12-08.prereq.1: Reading the numbers in a table
y-m-12-08.s.s1.prompt: Group 가 wants to find the month with the most books borrowed and the month with the fewest. Which graph is suitable?
y-m-12-08.s.s1.hint.0: First say whether what you want to find is 'change' or 'comparing sizes'.
y-m-12-08.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine how easy it is to find the highest place in each of the two graphs.
y-m-12-08.s.s1.o.a: Bar graph: it is easy to compare the heights of the bars with each other
y-m-12-08.s.s1.r.a: You gave a reason that fits the purpose of comparing the sizes of the months side by side.
y-m-12-08.s.s1.o.b: Line graph: you can also find the months with the most and the fewest by the heights of the points
y-m-12-08.s.s1.r.b: You pointed out that you can also compare by the heights of the points. This is suitable too.
y-m-12-08.s.s1.o.c: Neither is suitable. With as many as 12 values you can't show it in a graph
y-m-12-08.s.s1.r.c: You can show about 12 values in a graph. Having many numbers in the table does not make it impossible.
y-m-12-08.s.s1.explain: For finding the months with the most and fewest, comparing the heights of the bars is easy. A line graph can also find them by the heights of the points, so it can be seen as suitable too.
y-m-12-08.s.s1.acc.0: You can also find the months with the most and fewest by the heights of the points. The bar graph is just easier for comparing heights.
y-m-12-08.s.s2.prompt: Group 나 wants to see at a glance how it goes up and down as months pass. Which graph would they choose, and what is the reason?
y-m-12-08.s.s2.hint.0: Compare how the sudden drop in the number of books in July and August would look in each of the two graphs.
y-m-12-08.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what 'seen at a glance' means and which of lines or bars shows it better.
y-m-12-08.s.s2.o.a: Bar graph: because you can tell right away that the higher the bar, the more were borrowed, and it is easy to compare sizes
y-m-12-08.s.s2.r.a: It is good for comparing sizes, but you have not yet said the purpose of seeing change between months.
y-m-12-08.s.s2.o.b: Both are the same. Only the shape of the graph is different, and what you can know and how easy it is to read are the same
y-m-12-08.s.s2.r.b: Even if the facts you can know are the same, what is seen at a glance is different. Compare which shape shows change better.
y-m-12-08.s.s2.o.c: Line graph: the change can be seen in how the line joining the points goes up and down
y-m-12-08.s.s2.r.c: You pointed out that change can be read as the line going up and down.
y-m-12-08.s.s2.explain: How things change as months pass shows at a glance in the up and down of the line joining the points. You can also read change from a bar graph, but how connected it looks is different.
y-m-12-08.s.s2.acc.0: You can read the change in height from month to month in a bar graph too. But it is the line graph that shows the change in a connected way.
y-m-12-08.s.s3.prompt: Looking at the graph, the number of books was especially small in July (20 books) and August (12 books). A friend said, 'It's low because of vacation.' Can the graph or table alone tell the reason? Write separately what you can know for sure from the graph and what you need to find out more about.
y-m-12-08.s.s3.hint.0: First write the numbers you can read from the graph.
y-m-12-08.s.s3.hint.1: To check whether the vacation claim is right, think of just one date or question that would be needed.
y-m-12-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the sure things (numbers) and the guess (reason) separately?
y-m-12-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: To check the claim that it is because of vacation, did you write specifically what more data is needed?
y-m-12-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think that there could be other reasons?
y-m-12-08.s.s3.model.0: What is sure from the graph is that few books were borrowed: 20 in July and 12 in August. The graph alone can't tell whether it was because of vacation; I'd need to find out how many days students were at school then or ask the students.
y-m-12-08.s.s3.model.1: You can see in the table that few books were borrowed in July and August. But it is not certain whether the reason is vacation. You can check by investigating more about the vacation dates and the number of days the library was open.
y-m-12-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: It wrote the reason and the needed data separately.

y-m-12-09.title: A table where 'Other' is the biggest
y-m-12-09.topic: Deciding the categories for sorting data (the 'Other' category)
y-m-12-09.goal: Find out the problem with a table in which the 'Other' cell is the biggest, and make several ways to organize the same data more usefully by splitting up the categories.
y-m-12-09.material: 24 fourth-graders were each asked the one activity they most want to do during break. Everyone chose just one. Jiyun set the categories as soccer, reading, drawing, and Other (activities besides these), and organized them in a table. The result is soccer 6 people, reading 5 people, drawing 4 people, Other 9 people (24 people in total). Jiyun said, 'Other is the most!' The activities the 9 'Other' people chose are jump rope, tag, board games, and so on.
y-m-12-09.thinking.0: Finding the design problem of a table
y-m-12-09.thinking.1: Making several ways of organizing under constraints
y-m-12-09.prereq.0: Counting data by category and organizing it in a table
y-m-12-09.prereq.1: The total of a table must equal the number of people surveyed
y-m-12-09.s.s1.prompt: How should we think about Other being the most in this table?
y-m-12-09.s.s1.hint.0: Think of the activities the 9 Other people chose one by one. Are there several friends who chose the same activity?
y-m-12-09.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what the person looking at the table would be most curious about.
y-m-12-09.s.s1.o.a: You can tell that the Other activity is the most popular, so Jiyun organized the table very well
y-m-12-09.s.s1.r.a: 'Other' is a cell that bundles several activities. It is not one activity that is popular.
y-m-12-09.s.s1.o.b: If Other is the biggest, you can't tell what they want to do, so it is better to split the categories further
y-m-12-09.s.s1.r.b: You pointed out that when a bundled cell is big, the information you want to know is hidden.
y-m-12-09.s.s1.o.c: The total is exactly 24 people, so there is nothing to fix in the table
y-m-12-09.s.s1.r.c: The total being right and the table being useful are different.
y-m-12-09.s.s1.o.d: If you remove the Other cell, every student chooses one of the four
y-m-12-09.s.s1.r.d: If you remove Other, there is nowhere in the table to put the activities those 9 people chose.
y-m-12-09.s.s1.explain: If Other is the biggest, you can't tell what is popular. If you split the activities the 9 people chose into categories, the table becomes more useful. Whether the total is right is a separate matter.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.prompt: Split the 9 Other people again into jump rope (g1 people), tag (g2 people), and Other (h people), and make a new table. The conditions are as follows. All three cells have 1 or more people, and the total is 9 people. And 'Other' must not be more than any of the other cells (soccer 6, reading 5, drawing 4, jump rope, tag). Make 3 different tables.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.hint.0: Decide jump rope and tag first so that the three cells add up to 9, and make the remaining number Other.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.hint.1: Compare, one at a time, with jump rope, tag, and drawing (4 people) to check that Other does not become bigger than the other cells.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.ok.c1: All three cells are natural numbers that are 1 or more.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.fail.c1: All three cells must be natural numbers that are 1 or more.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the three cells is not 9 people.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.ok.c3: Other is not more than all the other cells.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.fail.c3: Other is more than one of the cells: jump rope, tag, or drawing (4 people).
y-m-12-09.s.s2.explain: For example, with jump rope 4 people, tag 4 people, Other 1 person, the total is 9 and Other is the smallest. Other can also be equal and still fit the conditions, as in jump rope 3, tag 3, Other 3. If you make Other 0 people, it is a problem when there is a student who chose an 'activity besides these' (so I made it 1 or more).
y-m-12-09.s.s2.because.prompt: Write in one sentence why it is good not to make the Other cell the biggest.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Think about what a friend looking at the table could find out when Other is the biggest.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about what activities are mixed in the Other cell.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does the reason you wrote connect to 'what the person looking at the table can know'?
y-m-12-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you also think about the reason for not removing Other completely?
y-m-12-09.s.s2.because.model.0: If Other is the biggest, you can't tell what the students really want to do. Activities that come up a lot need their own cell so you can see which activities are popular.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.because.model.1: If the Other cell is big, detailed information is hidden, so the person reading the table can't find out what they are curious about.
y-m-12-09.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: It mentioned that information is hidden.

y-m-12-10.title: Can we know the value of the hidden bar?
y-m-12-10.topic: Finding a hidden value in a bar graph (checking the conditions)
y-m-12-10.goal: Understand that finding a hidden value from the total needs conditions such as 'each person chose only one', and make several possible values when the conditions are different.
y-m-12-10.material: Yeoreum's class surveyed their favorite snacks and showed them in a bar graph. But the tteokbokki bar is covered by paper and cannot be seen. The visible bars are fruit 7 people, bread 5 people, ice cream 8 people, Other 3 people (23 people in total). Yeoreum's class has 25 people. Yeoreum said, 'If you subtract 23 from 25, tteokbokki is 2 people.' You have not been told yet about how the survey was done.
y-m-12-10.thinking.1: Judging whether the conclusion changes when the conditions change
y-m-12-10.thinking.2: Making several values that fit the conditions
y-m-12-10.prereq.0: In a bar graph, one bar shows the number of students for one category
y-m-12-10.s.s1.prompt: For Yeoreum's words to be right, what must be true?
y-m-12-10.s.s1.hint.0: Think about what the total should be if all 25 people go into only one bar each.
y-m-12-10.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine what the total would be if one person chose two things.
y-m-12-10.s.s1.o.a: The tteokbokki bar must be the shortest of the five bars
y-m-12-10.s.s1.r.a: The order of the bar lengths has nothing to do with the sum of the number of students.
y-m-12-10.s.s1.o.b: The heights of the four visible bars must all be different values
y-m-12-10.s.s1.r.b: The heights can be the same or different. It has nothing to do with the total.
y-m-12-10.s.s1.o.c: Knowing that the class has 25 students is enough and no other information is needed
y-m-12-10.s.s1.r.c: The number of students alone is not enough. You must also check whether every student chose only one thing and whether no student is missing.
y-m-12-10.s.s1.o.d: Everyone must have chosen only one thing and no student must be missing from the survey
y-m-12-10.s.s1.r.d: You pointed out that these two conditions are needed for the total to equal the number of students.
y-m-12-10.s.s1.explain: If all 25 people chose one thing each, the total is 25 and tteokbokki is 2 people. If one student chose two things or there is a student who was not surveyed, the total will not be 25.
y-m-12-10.s.s2.prompt: How many of the following must you definitely check in order to fix the number of tteokbokki students as 2 people? Choose all that are suitable.
y-m-12-10.s.s2.hint.0: Suppose a situation in which all 25 people were counted exactly once. What would happen to break that assumption?
y-m-12-10.s.s2.hint.1: Check one by one whether each choice guarantees or breaks 'total = 25'.
y-m-12-10.s.s2.o.a: Each person chose only one thing
y-m-12-10.s.s2.r.a: If one person can choose two things, the total can become bigger than the number of students. It is a needed condition.
y-m-12-10.s.s2.o.b: There is no student who was absent on the survey day and could not take part in the survey
y-m-12-10.s.s2.r.b: If there is a student who could not take part, the total can become less than 25. It is a needed condition.
y-m-12-10.s.s2.o.c: More students chose tteokbokki than Other (3 people)
y-m-12-10.s.s2.r.c: This is a comparison unrelated to whether tteokbokki is fixed as 2 people.
y-m-12-10.s.s2.o.d: The title of the graph says 'favorite snack'
y-m-12-10.s.s2.r.d: A title does not guarantee that the total equals the number of students.
y-m-12-10.s.s2.explain: To find it by subtracting from the total, every student must go into a bar exactly once. Both of two things are needed: each person chose only one thing, and no student is missing from the survey.
y-m-12-10.s.s3.prompt: This time, each person could choose up to two things, and suppose all 25 people chose at least one. In this case, make 3 examples of what the number of tteokbokki students t and the number of students who chose two things m could be, so that the t values are different. (The sum of the four visible bars, 23 people, stays the same.)
y-m-12-10.s.s3.hint.0: Think about how much the bar total increases each time one more student chooses two things.
y-m-12-10.s.s3.hint.1: Decide m first, and then adjust t so that the bar total is 25+m.
y-m-12-10.s.s3.var.m: Number of students who chose two things (people)
y-m-12-10.s.s3.ok.c1: The number of students is a natural number that is 0 or more.
y-m-12-10.s.s3.fail.c1: Write the number of students as a natural number that is 0 or more.
y-m-12-10.s.s3.ok.c2: The number of students in one cell does not go over the whole class (25 people).
y-m-12-10.s.s3.fail.c2: The number of tteokbokki students or of students who chose two things cannot be over 25 people.
y-m-12-10.s.s3.ok.c3: The sum of the bars equals 25 plus the number of students who chose two things.
y-m-12-10.s.s3.fail.c3: The bar total (23+t) is not equal to 25+m.
y-m-12-10.s.s3.explain: If one person chooses two things, the bar total becomes greater than 25. The total is 25+m, so t=2+m. If m is 0, t=2, and if m is 3, t=5, so t can be several different values. So if you don't know how the survey was done, you can't fix the number of tteokbokki students as one value.

y-m-12-11.title: Can the result of asking 10 people tell us about the whole grade?
y-m-12-11.topic: How to choose who to survey (who should you ask so you can speak about the whole grade?)
y-m-12-11.goal: Understand that the range you can claim from the same result differs depending on whether the people surveyed represent the whole, and revise your judgment with new information.
y-m-12-11.material: There are 100 fourth-graders in Minho's school. Minho wants to find out 'the sport that fourth-graders like best'. He asks them to choose only one sport. How far you can trust the result depends on how Minho chose who to survey.
y-m-12-11.thinking.0: Noticing the limits of how the data was collected
y-m-12-11.thinking.1: Revising how sure you are with new information
y-m-12-11.thinking.2: Choosing a more trustworthy survey method
y-m-12-11.prereq.0: Showing survey results with tables and bar graphs
y-m-12-11.prereq.1: The difference between 'the whole' and 'a part'
y-m-12-11.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what you can say about 'the whole 4th grade'.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.hint.0: First sort out what kind of people the surveyed people are.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether the new information changes the numbers or changes how to interpret the numbers.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.0.info: Minho asked 10 friends who sat together with him at lunchtime. The result is soccer 7 people, basketball 2 people, running 1 person.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.0.ask: From this result, can you say 'in the whole 4th grade, soccer is liked best'?
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.0.after: It is a clear fact that 7 of 10 chose soccer. But to speak about the whole 4th grade, you need to look at whether those 10 represent the whole well.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Yes. 7 out of 10, so the whole 4th grade will probably also have soccer the most, similarly
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.0.r.a: There is not yet a ground for widening the result of 10 people to all 100. Who these 10 are matters.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Soccer came out the most, but it is only 10 friends who sat together, so the whole 4th grade is not certain yet
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You told apart the result of a part and the whole.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Can't say. 10 is small compared to 100, so it is completely useless
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The result of 10 people is also information. It is just not enough to speak about 'the whole'.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.1.info: It turned out that the 10 who sat together at lunchtime were all friends from the same soccer club.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.1.ask: After learning this information, what happens to your thinking about the whole 4th grade?
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.1.after: Your first judgment was 'not certain yet', so it is fine to keep it, and it is also fine to say the reason is now clearer. What matters is that it is hard to speak about the whole 4th grade from the result of these 10.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Soccer is the most. Even if some are from a soccer club, it is a fact that 7 people chose it
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.1.r.a: It is a fact that 7 people chose it, but the ground for widening it to the whole 4th grade got weaker.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Now it is hard to trust as a result for the whole 4th grade. These 10 are a group likely to like soccer
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You noticed that the people surveyed may be leaning one way.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.1.o.c: My thought that it is not certain as at first stays, and the reason has become clearer
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You kept your first judgment and sorted out that the reason became firmer with the new information.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It means that there are no students in 4th grade who like soccer
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.1.r.d: From the group of these 10 alone, the conclusion 'there is nobody' does not follow.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.2.info: Minho again chose 20 students by drawing numbers, 4 from each of classes 1 to 5 of 4th grade, and asked them. The result is soccer 6 people, basketball 5 people, running 4 people, jump rope 3 people, Other 2 people.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.2.ask: What can you say from the result of these 20?
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.2.after: The same number from each class was chosen by drawing numbers, so it represents the whole 4th grade better than the earlier survey. Still, the difference between soccer and basketball is small, so it is hard to claim, and asking more students would make it more certain.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Soccer is the most. You can say that it is liked best in the whole 4th grade too
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.2.r.a: 6 people and 5 people differ by a small amount. It is too early to claim just because it came out more.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Soccer is slightly ahead, but 6 people and 5 people differ by a small amount, so it is hard to claim it is liked best
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.2.r.b: From data with better representativeness, you also considered the size of the difference.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Basketball is the hidden number 1. Because it differs by class
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.2.r.c: There is no ground. In the data, soccer is 1 person more.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.2.o.d: You can see that soccer is a little more, and asking more students would make it more certain
y-m-12-11.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You said only as much as the current data lets you say, and also said how to make it more certain.
y-m-12-11.s.s1.reflect: The result of the first 10 was 'not certain yet', and when the information about the soccer club came, the reason became clear. When surveyed by another method, the result changed and the range of what you could say widened a little. Notice that even with the same numbers, what you can say differs depending on 'whom you asked'.
y-m-12-11.s.s2.prompt: Even if you survey the same 20 people, which method is most suitable for representing the whole 4th grade better?
y-m-12-11.s.s2.hint.0: For each method, imagine one by one whether the friends picked would look like the whole 4th grade.
y-m-12-11.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether it is a method where only friends from one class are picked, or a method where every class is picked.
y-m-12-11.s.s2.o.a: Ask the first 20 people you meet near the soccer goal on the playground
y-m-12-11.s.s2.r.a: Near the soccer goal there may be more students who like soccer.
y-m-12-11.s.s2.o.b: Pick the same number from each class by drawing numbers
y-m-12-11.s.s2.r.b: Every student has a chance of being picked, and the leaning between classes gets smaller.
y-m-12-11.s.s2.o.c: Ask the same friends the same question twice and collect 40 answers
y-m-12-11.s.s2.r.c: If you ask the same people again, only the number of answers increases, and the number of new people's thoughts does not.
y-m-12-11.s.s2.o.d: Ask the first 20 students who raise their hands among those who raised their hands
y-m-12-11.s.s2.r.d: Students who raise their hands may be students who like to speak. Not all students have the same chance.
y-m-12-11.s.s2.explain: If you draw numbers so that whom you ask spreads evenly, and pick the same number from each class, it is hard to lean to one side. The other methods lean toward people on one side or do not increase the number of people.

y-m-12-12.title: The top of two classes and the top of the whole grade
y-m-12-12.topic: Reading two tables together (the top of each class and the top of the whole grade)
y-m-12-12.goal: Make an example yourself to check that the item that is first in each class cannot be said to be first in the combined result of both classes, and explain why the combined table is needed.
y-m-12-12.material: Class 가 and Class 나 of 4th grade each asked 20 people for the one sport they like. There are only three items, soccer, basketball, and dodgeball, and everyone chose just one. In Class 가, soccer was the most (clearly more than the other two), and in Class 나, basketball was the most (clearly more than the other two). The teacher asked, 'In the grade result combining both classes, would one of soccer or basketball be first?'
y-m-12-12.thinking.0: Making a counterexample to see if a generalization holds
y-m-12-12.thinking.1: Finding numbers that satisfy several conditions at once
y-m-12-12.thinking.2: Explaining the reason for reading them combined
y-m-12-12.prereq.0: Reading a table by item and adding
y-m-12-12.prereq.1: Finding the item with the most
y-m-12-12.s.s1.prompt: What is the most suitable way to answer the teacher's question?
y-m-12-12.s.s1.hint.0: Recall that the numbers for items that are not first in each class are also included in the total.
y-m-12-12.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine what the total would be if soccer and basketball take turns being first in each class but dodgeball is always second or third.
y-m-12-12.s.s1.o.a: One of soccer or basketball is definitely first. Because the item first in each class is also first when combined
y-m-12-12.s.s1.r.a: Even if it is first in each class, it is not guaranteed to be first when combined. Test it with numbers.
y-m-12-12.s.s1.o.b: When combined, the firsts of both classes become the same number of people and it's a tie
y-m-12-12.s.s1.r.b: Combining does not necessarily make a tie. You can only find out by adding item by item.
y-m-12-12.s.s1.o.c: Make numbers and test whether a table in which dodgeball is first is possible
y-m-12-12.s.s1.r.c: This is an attitude of directly testing whether a counterexample is possible instead of a general feeling.
y-m-12-12.s.s1.o.d: Combining is meaningless. Looking at each class separately is enough
y-m-12-12.s.s1.r.d: When you want to know the result of the whole grade, you need the combined table.
y-m-12-12.s.s1.explain: There is no guarantee that the first in each class equals the first in the combined table. You can check by actually making numbers that make dodgeball first.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.prompt: Let the numbers of people for soccer, basketball, and dodgeball in Class 가 be a1, a2, a3, and in Class 나 be b1, b2, b3. Make 2 different tables in which dodgeball is first when the two classes are combined. Each class has 20 people in total, and Class 가 must have soccer clearly more than the other two, and Class 나 must have basketball clearly more than the other two. In the combined table, dodgeball must also be clearly more than the other two.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.hint.0: Dodgeball must be second most, close to first, in both classes. First set one class's dodgeball to 1~2 people fewer than the first.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate the totals of soccer, basketball, and dodgeball when combined, and check whether dodgeball is the largest.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.ok.c1: All numbers of people are natural numbers that are 0 or more.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.fail.c1: Write all numbers of people as natural numbers that are 0 or more.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.ok.c2: Both classes have a total of 20 people.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.fail.c2: One class's total is not 20 people.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.ok.c3: In Class 가, soccer is the most.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.fail.c3: In Class 가, soccer is not more than the other two.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.ok.c4: In Class 나, basketball is the most.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.fail.c4: In Class 나, basketball is not more than the other two.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.ok.c5: In the combined table, dodgeball is the most.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.fail.c5: In the combined table, dodgeball is not more than soccer or basketball.
y-m-12-12.s.s2.explain: For example, if Class 가 has soccer 8, basketball 5, dodgeball 7 and Class 나 has soccer 5, basketball 8, dodgeball 7, the combined table is soccer 13, basketball 13, dodgeball 14, so dodgeball is first. The first in each class may not be first in the combined table.
y-m-12-12.s.s3.prompt: What does this result tell you about the idea 'if you know the first in each class, you can know the first in the whole grade'? Also write what information you need to know the first in the whole grade.
y-m-12-12.s.s3.hint.0: In the table you made, check what rank dodgeball had in each class.
y-m-12-12.s.s3.hint.1: Look at whether the numbers for items that are not first were also used when finding the total.
y-m-12-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you connect the statement 'the first in each class is not necessarily the first in the grade' to your number example?
y-m-12-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the needed information is all the numbers of people by item in each class (not only the first)?
y-m-12-12.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Does it include the statement that you check by adding?
y-m-12-12.s.s3.model.0: You can't say the first in each class is also first when combined. In my example, dodgeball was second in both classes, but when I combined them it was first. To know the whole grade, you have to add up the numbers by item for the two classes and look.
y-m-12-12.s.s3.model.1: Even if an item is first in each class, the combined result can change. You need to know all the numbers of people by item, not only the first, and you need to add the two classes' values for the same items and compare.
